Kingda Ka was a hydraulically-launched [steel roller coaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel_roller_coaster) located at [Six Flags Great Adventure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six_Flags_Great_Adventure) in [Jackson, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_New_Jersey), United States. Manufactured by [Intamin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intamin) and designed by [Werner Stengel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werner_Stengel), Kingda Ka opened as the [tallest and fastest roller coaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_roller_coaster_rankings) in the world on May 21, 2005, surpassing [Top Thrill Dragster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_Thrill_Dragster) at [Cedar Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Point). Although both featured similar designs, Kingda Ka's layout added an [airtime hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airtime_hill) on the return portion of the track. It was also the second [strata coaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strata_coaster) ever built, exceeding 400 feet (120 m) in height.

The ride used a [hydraulic launch mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accelerator_Coaster#Technology) to accelerate the train up to 128 mph (206 km/h) in 3.5 seconds. While [Formula Rossa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formula_Rossa) at [Ferrari World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrari_World) broke its speed record in 2010, Kingda Ka remained the tallest in the world throughout its operational lifespan. The record-breaking coaster featured a 456-foot-tall (139 m) [top hat tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roller_coaster_elements#Top_hat) with a 418-foot (127 m) drop, which separately ranked as the longest drop in the world.

In November 2024, following months of rumors and speculation regarding the future of the attraction, Six Flags Great Adventure announced that Kingda Ka had permanently closed. The ride was demolished and removed from the park.

Kingda Ka was officially unveiled on September 29, 2004, and was scheduled to open at [Six Flags Great Adventure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six_Flags_Great_Adventure) in 2005.[[1]](#cite_note-ThrillNetwork-Announcement-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Berland_2004-2) The announcement was made at a media event held for roller coaster enthusiasts and [the press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_press).[[1]](#cite_note-ThrillNetwork-Announcement-1) Six Flags billed the new ride as "the tallest and fastest roller coaster on earth", with a height of 456 feet (139 m) and the ability to accelerate to 128 mph (206 km/h) in 3.5 seconds.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

The ride would be part of a new themed area called the Golden Kingdom, an 11-acre (4.5 ha) section already under development in the park. [Six Flags](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six_Flags) CEO Kieran Burke at the time stated, "This is the first step in a process of really transforming Six Flags Great Adventure from the largest regional theme park in the world to a true regional destination."[[2]](#cite_note-Berland_2004-2)

115-== Incidents ==
116-
117-On June 8, 2005, a bolt failed inside a trough through which the launch cable travels. This caused the liner to come loose, creating friction on the cable and preventing the train from accelerating to the correct speed. The cable rubbing against the trough caused sparks and shards of metal to fly out from the bottom of the train.<ref>{{cite news |title=2005 incident |website=RideAccidents.com |date=2005 |url=http://www.rideaccidents.com/2005.html#jun8 |access-date=June 4, 2012 |archive-date=July 18, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120718060107/http://www.rideaccidents.com/2005.html#jun8 |url-status=live}}</ref> Damage occurred to the launch cable, which was frayed and required replacement, including minor damage to seals and brake fins.<!-- Although source is reliable, about.com is blacklisted.
